_readme: The record behind civic/the-money-in-the-air/. Edit figures here, then run: python3 build.py (in this folder). Every figure: v (dollars, or a count), date (when the source published it), through (the last day the figure covers), src (source ids, in 'sources' below), tag (VERIFIED: filing or page read directly; REPORTED: a named outlet carried it, or the page was not read in full). 'bought' is the what-this-bought line, only where a tracker or filing gives it. A district or figure with status 'refresh' renders as 'Refresh Thursday' until it is filled. Text may carry [[c:id]] citation tokens; numbers are assigned at build time in order of first use.

meta.title: The money in the air
meta.headline: $423 million in ads on one Ohio Senate race.

cycles.note: Democrats outspent Republicans, $57 million to $49.5 million.

cycles.note: The most for any race other than a presidential one, on AdImpact's record.
cycles.bought: More than 222,000 broadcast airings, about 120,000 Democratic and 102,000 Republican. Cleveland was the top market at $132.9 million. Google ads: $29.9 million. [[c:adimpact-2024]]

cycles.note: A special election for the two years left in the term. 2024 was a six-year seat in a presidential year.
cycles.bought: By October 15, Democratic advertisers had aired 200 more broadcast spots than Republican ones; the report attributes the gap to lower candidate ad rates. [[c:spectrum-oct15]] Republican spending passed $30 million in a single week. [[c:ocj-oct20]] Cleveland was the second-largest political ad market in the country for the two weeks ending August 14, at $10.5 million. [[c:insideradio-aug19]]

ai.ohio: April 2026: a Republican-aligned super PAC released a spot showing an AI-generated Sherrod Brown at the end of a birthday party, ending "Party's over, Sherrod." The Washington Post and Al Jazeera, which described it, did not name the committee that paid for it. [[c:wapo-sep30]] [[c:aljazeera-oct9]]
ai.law: As of October 5, Ohio was listed among 20 states with no law on political deepfakes. [[c:politicalgroup]] Two bills, House Bill 362 and House Bill 1000, have been introduced in the 136th General Assembly; neither has been reported as passed. [[c:hb362]] [[c:hb1000]]
ai.fec: September 19, 2024: the FEC declined to write a new rule on AI in campaign ads and said its existing ban on fraudulent misrepresentation applies whatever the technology. [[c:fec-ai-2024]]

week.text: FEC October Quarterly reports due, covering through September 30. AdImpact's Senate count: $423 million.
63 outside committees have reported $293.25 million in the Senate general election to the FEC.
No Going Back PAC and Safety & Affordability PAC e-file their first reports of receipts: $200 million and $25 million from MAGA Inc. The FEC had processed both by October 23.

The Ramaswamy campaign confirms it produced a one-minute video featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother, says it will spend $4 million to air it on television and online, and says the woman was not paid. The video first circulated without the "paid for" tag that is legally required for an ad to air on television.
At a rally in Sharonville, Ramaswamy does not address the ad in his remarks. Vice President JD Vance, speaking after him, defends it: "Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial."
Ohio pre-general reports due at 4 p.m. for state candidates and issue committees, including the race for governor.
FEC pre-general reports due, covering October 1 to 14.
67 outside committees have reported $349.3 million in the Senate general election to the FEC.

rules.federal: Ads that support or oppose a federal candidate must say who paid. On television, an ad paid for by anyone other than the candidate must say aloud that the payer "is responsible for the content of this advertising" and show a written statement at least 4 percent of the screen's height for at least 4 seconds. [[c:cfr-110-11]] [[c:usc-30120]]
rules.ohio: Ohio's disclaimer law, in its current version since September 30, 2025: anyone who pays for political advertising for or against an Ohio candidate or issue must identify itself on the ad; when a candidate or campaign pays, the line begins "paid for by"; broadcasters and printers may not run paid political ads without it. [[c:orc-3517-20]]
rules.c4: A 501(c)(4) nonprofit may give to a super PAC without naming its own donors. One Nation gave Senate Leadership Fund $132.9 million this cycle. On air, the ad names Senate Leadership Fund. [[c:votelog]]
rules.late: No Going Back PAC, formed September 1, had reported $159.6 million in spending across its races by October 14 before any receipts were on file [[c:legis1-oct14]]; its first two reports, e-filed October 20 (the October monthly, covering September, and the pre-general, covering October 1 to 14), list $200 million from MAGA Inc. [[c:fec-ngb]] Enough Promises Ohio PAC, formed September 29, had not disclosed its contributors by October 12 [[c:ap-oct12]]; its pre-general report, e-filed October 22, lists one, Conservative Americans PAC, at $2.5 million. [[c:fec-epo]]
rules.state_gap: Ohio's pre-general report, due October 22, covers activity through October 14. From October 15 through Election Day, the campaign of the candidates for governor and lieutenant governor must also file a statement within two business days whenever one contributor's gifts in that period reach $10,000. [[c:orc-3517-10]] Money that passes through a state committee shows that committee's donors: Ohioans For Lower Costs shows $1 million from the IBEW. [[c:ocj-oct20]]
